title: Nets, surface area, volume and 3D views
transcript: A net shows the flat faces that can fold around a solid. Surface area adds the faces the object actually has. Volume counts how much fills the object. For a rectangular box it is the base area times the height.

An AMC practice problem can ask which net folds to a box or how much card it needs. Label matching edge lengths on the net. A Rossmoyne style problem may fix volume and ask for the least surface area. Use the volume to constrain the possible dimensions first.
A rectangular block is four units long, three units wide and two units high. Find its volume in cubic units. Think of the base footprint repeating in every layer.
One unit-high layer contains twelve cubes because the base is four by three. With two full layers, the volume is twenty-four cubic units.
An open-top box has base five by three and height two units. Ignore thickness and tabs. How much card is needed for the base and its walls? Match each wall with the corresponding side of the base.

Start with base area fifteen. Two walls have width five and the other two have width three. The height is the same for all walls. Add the base and four walls only. The card area is forty-seven square units.

An open-top rectangular box has height three centimetres and capacity one hundred and eight cubic centimetres. Its base sides must be positive integers. Find the least card area, including the base and the four walls. Ignore tabs and thickness.

Divide the volume by the height. Every legal base has area thirty-six, so the base sides must be a factor pair of thirty-six. With base sides a and b, the wall area is twice the height times the sum of a and b. The base contributes the same amount in every case. Compare the sums for the complete list of factor pairs. The smallest sum comes from six and six.

The resulting total card area is one hundred and eight square centimetres. This includes only the base and the walls. Each unordered factor pair is listed by its shorter side, which cannot exceed the square root of the base area. Therefore no allowed dimensions are missing.

A box without a lid has five faces made of card. Do not include a second copy of the base. Volume measures cubic units, while surface area measures square units. Read which of those quantities is fixed and which you need to find.

Draw the net and label matching sides. List each face that contributes material, even when no diagram is given. For fixed volume, divide by height and check the possible base factor pairs. Compare the surface area rather than comparing the lengths alone.
